newsitem.title: USA: Schwarzkopf doubts Gulf War troops exposed to gas.
newsitem.headline: Schwarzkopf doubts Gulf War troops exposed to gas.

text.p: Gulf War commander Norman Schwarzkopf said on Thursday he doubted U.S. troops were exposed to Iraqi war gas because a milligram of it is fatal and he got no report throughout the war that anyone was even sickened by gas.

"We never ever ever had a single report of any symptoms (of war gas exposure) at all on the part of 541,000 Americans over there and 800,000 allies," Schwarzkopf told the Senate Armed Services Committee.

"So my sense of logic just says, look if we're talking about something where one milligram can cause a fatality then certainly somewhere along the way if this stuff had affected our troops somebody would have come up with these symptoms, and they didn't," he said.

The retired general said he was therefore shocked when the Defence Department announced last year that up to 20,000 U.S. Gulf War veterans may have been exposed to gas when U.S. demolition teams blew up an Iraqi weapons dump containing chemical weapons just after the 1991 war.

He said Saudi Defence Minister Prince Sultan told him on Wednesday that there were also no reports during the war or since that Saudi, Iraqi or Kuwaiti civilians suffered symptoms of exposure to war gas.

The retired commander said he could shed little light on a Pentagon disclosure this week that the CIA warned U.S. units before they blew up the Kamisiyah dump containing Iraqi war gas that such weapons might be there.

He said he assumed the Feb. 26, 1991, warning went through his headquarters but it was during the five-day ground war, a day after an Iraqi Scud missile killed 28 U.S. soldiers, and hundreds of messages were flowing through his headquarters.

The Pentagon said this week the warning did not get to the specific Army units that blew up the Kamisiyah arms dump, but Schwarzkopf said he assumed, without knowing, that such a warning would go to all units in the area. "I have no idea whether it did or not," he testified. "I would assume it did because ... we considered every ammunition dump at that time to be a suspected ammunition chemical storage area."
President Bill Clinton ordered his Presidential Advisory Committee on Gulf War Veterans Illnesses on Wednesday to investigate the warning.

Deputy Defence Secretary John White said at the Senate hearing that he had also ordered a Defence Department investigation of who received the warning and whether it got to the units that blew up the Kamisiyah site, for whom a warning would have been most critical.
The CIA said its warning did not say specifically that chemical weapons might be at Kamisiyah but said there was raw, unconfirmed intelligence such weapons may be in that region.
